title: The Social Contract
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
openingChapterLabel: Book 1, Chapter 1 — Subject of the First Book
openingText:
_Author’s prefatory notice_

This short treatise is an extract from a larger work, begun some time ago without measuring my abilities and long since abandoned. Of the various pieces that could be taken from what was completed, this is the most substantial and seemed to me the least unworthy of being offered to the public. The rest no longer exists.

_Book I_

I want to ask whether, in the civil order, there can be any sure and legitimate rule of administration — taking men as they are and laws as they might be. In this inquiry I will always try to unite what right sanctions with what is prescribed by interest, so that justice and utility are never divided.
about:
What makes political authority legitimate? Rousseau asks how people can form a society and live under common laws without surrendering their freedom. His answer turns on the social contract and the general will: a will directed toward the common good, distinct from a mere sum of private wishes.

The four books examine the foundation of political society, sovereignty and legislation, forms of government, and citizens’ participation in public life. Throughout, Rousseau distinguishes the people as sovereign from the government that carries out the laws. The later chapters discuss Roman assemblies, dictatorship, censorship, and civil religion; a short conclusion identifies further subjects beyond this work’s scope.

Follow the tensions between individual and community, consent and coercion, and religious tolerance and a shared civic creed. Historical examples form part of the argument and reflect the author’s own period and sources.

angleCards.title: The general will
angleCards.text: When does a decision express the common good? Follow the distinction between the general will, the will of all, and particular interests, and ask why a majority can be mistaken.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine Rousseau’s definition of the general will and the conditions under which a vote can express it.

angleCards.title: Freedom and coercion
angleCards.text: In Book I, Rousseau says that someone who refuses to obey the general will can be forced to be free. Read this alongside his distinctions between natural, civil, and moral liberty.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to assess Rousseau’s argument about freedom and obligation and test his justification of political coercion.

angleCards.title: The lawgiver and the people
angleCards.text: The lawgiver designs institutions without possessing the sovereign right to enact laws. How can a people judge an order that has not yet shaped them?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the tension between the lawgiver’s guidance and the people’s authority to enact their own laws.

angleCards.title: Civil religion
angleCards.text: Rousseau proposes a shared civic profession of faith and tolerance for religions that tolerate others. He also permits banishment and, in a specified case, execution.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how civil religion fits with the book’s principles of freedom, community, and sovereignty.

cast.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
cast.description: The author investigates the grounds of legitimate political authority. He writes as a citizen of a free state and explains his interest in politics through his right to vote.

cast.name: The General Will
cast.description: The will directed toward the community’s interest. Rousseau distinguishes it from a sum of private interests and from an actual decision that may result from deception.

cast.name: The Sovereign
cast.description: The collective body formed by the social contract. It enacts general laws and must be distinguished from the government that executes them.

cast.name: The Lawgiver
cast.description: The figure who proposes a people’s fundamental order without holding sovereign legislative power. Rousseau examines the role especially in Book II.

cast.name: The Government
cast.description: The intermediate body between sovereign and subjects. Rousseau examines democratic, aristocratic, and monarchical governments and their tendency to usurp sovereignty.

cast.name: The Citizen
cast.description: As a participant in sovereignty, the citizen helps make the laws; as a subject, the same person is bound by them. The relation between these roles is central to the argument.

whyItMatters.title: The grounds of authority
whyItMatters.body: Rousseau distinguishes the power to compel obedience from the right to demand it. The book therefore examines political legitimacy as well as the practical operation of governments.

whyItMatters.title: Speaking for the community
whyItMatters.body: The general will supplies a standard for collective decisions but raises the question of how to identify it. Discussions of factions, voting, and representation reveal the difficulties of connecting a principle to political institutions.

whyItMatters.title: The conditions of freedom
whyItMatters.body: The book asks what is gained and lost when natural independence gives way to society under common laws. It invites readers to examine the relationships between self-government, equality, obligation, and coercion.
